title: Caterpillar GNN: Replacing Message Passing with Graph-Level Aggregation
claim: Two structurally different pattern-counting notions, tree-like homomorphisms and colored walks, carry exactly the same expressive power.
layout: 2 panels joined by an equivalence sign, left-to-right, red arrows showing the mapping
description: Two small graph diagrams are joined by a large equivalence sign in the middle. On the left, a caterpillar tree F is labeled 'caterpillar'. Its spine nodes are green and its leaf nodes are pale. Red arrows run from each node of F to nodes of a gray triangle-with-tail graph G. The dark red arrows come from the spine nodes. The faint pink arrows come from the leaves and all land on the same node of G. A red φ marks the homomorphism. On the right, the same graph G is labeled 'degree coloring' with notation G, χ. Its nodes are colored red, blue and green by degree, and blue curved arrows trace a walk through them. Beside it a separate vertical path of colored nodes, labeled with a bold blue w, shows the colored walk as a sequence. The eye goes first to the red arrows on the left, then to the equivalence sign, then to the colored walk on the right.
caption: Counting over either of the two depicted notions is exactly as expressive on graphs. Left: A graph homomorphism $\varphi \colon F\to\, G$, where $F$ is a caterpillar graph. Right: An occurrence of a colored walk $\vw = \mathsf{brbg}$ in the same graph $G$ colored by $\chideg$ according to vertex degrees.
abstract: Message-passing graph neural networks (MPGNNs) dominate modern graph learning. Typical efforts enhance MPGNN's expressive power by enriching the adjacency-based aggregation. In contrast, we introduce a graph-level aggregation over walk incidence-based matrices that are constructed to deliberately trade off some expressivity for stronger and more structured inductive bias. This approach allows for gradual scaling between classical message-passing and simpler methods based on walks. Drawing on weighted automata, we ensure our gradual scaling is polynomial-time and avoids the combinatorial explosion of colored walks. Our second result characterizes the expressive power at each scale using homomorphism counts over a hierarchy of generalized caterpillar graphs. Based on these foundations, we propose Caterpillar GNNs that substantially reduce the number of nodes in the hidden layers of the computational graphs on real-world datasets. This gradual reduction does not obstruct learning, enabling a systematic study of lower-order expressivity. We further describe benchmark settings where task-aligned expressivity supports learning.
